## Definition

**Interval data** have equal distances between adjacent values, but no true zero point. Zero is arbitrary rather than representing the complete absence of the property.

## Characteristics

| Property | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| Equal intervals | 10-20 = same distance as 40-50 |
| No true zero | Zero is arbitrary, not "none" |
| Addition/subtraction | Meaningful operations |
| Ratios not meaningful | Can't say "twice as much" |

## Examples

| Variable | Why Interval |
|----------|--------------|
| Temperature (°C/°F) | 0°C ≠ absence of temperature; 40°C is not "twice as hot" as 20°C |
| IQ scores | 0 doesn't mean no intelligence; 140 isn't "twice as intelligent" as 70 |
| Calendar years | Year 0 is arbitrary; 2000 isn't "twice" 1000 |
| Standardised test scores | Zero is arbitrary |

## Why Ratios Don't Work

**Temperature example:**

- 20°C and 40°C
- Is 40°C "twice as hot"?
- Convert to Kelvin: 293K and 313K
- Now the ratio is 313/293 ≈ 1.07

The ratio changes with the scale because zero is arbitrary.

## Appropriate Statistics

| Statistic | Appropriate |
|-----------|-------------|
| Mean | ✓ |
| Standard deviation | ✓ |
| t-tests | ✓ |
| ANOVA | ✓ |
| Pearson's r | ✓ |
| Ratios | ✗ |

## Interval vs. Ratio

```
Interval (Temperature °C):
    │    │    │    │    │
   -10   0   10   20   30
        (arbitrary zero)

Ratio (Temperature Kelvin):
    │    │    │    │    │
    0   73   173  273  373
    (true zero: absolute zero)
```

## Practical Note

In psychology, most continuous data are treated as interval/ratio, including:

- Questionnaire totals
- Reaction times (actually ratio)
- Test scores

## DataLab Connection

Standardised scores from questionnaires at DataLab are interval data. You can calculate means and run t-tests, but avoid statements like "twice as anxious."
